title: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in a lung transplant recipient
case_prompt:
A 69-year-old man with end-stage COPD and pulmonary hypertension underwent bilateral lung transplantation. Induction immunosuppression was with basiliximab and high-dose methylprednisolone, followed by tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. Seven months post-transplant, he developed lethargy, gait instability, delayed speech, and declining pulmonary function tests. Empiric high-dose steroids for presumed acute rejection were given after a non-diagnostic bronchoalveolar lavage.

Over the next 2–3 weeks, he developed short-term memory loss, behavior changes, episodes of staring with confusion, limited verbal responses, and acute worsening of gait and aphasia. Neurologic examination showed inattention, delayed responses to questions, intermittent command following, tremors, and bilateral clonus; strength was preserved.

Head CT demonstrated bifrontal and right-greater-than-left temporal deep and subcortical white matter hypoattenuation, suggestive of a subacute white matter process. Brain MRI with and without contrast revealed abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintense signals in bilateral frontal, parietal, and temporal white matter (predominantly right frontal). 

On hospital Day 2, lumbar puncture showed 2 nucleated cells/μL, glucose 52 mg/dL (blood glucose 80 mg/dL), and protein 74.9 mg/dL. CSF cytology, Toxoplasma gondii PCR, EBV PCR, HSV-1 and HSV-2 PCR, and VDRL were negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered calcineurin inhibitor–induced toxic leukoencephalopathy (PRES) due to tacrolimus neurotoxicity — “calcineurin inhibitor‐induced toxic leukoencephalopathy which is type of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES)…”  
2. Considered post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease based on immunosuppressed state — “Our initial differential diagnosis included … post‐transplant lymphoproliferative disease…”  
3. Considered toxoplasmosis as an opportunistic CNS infection but ruled out by negative PCR — “CSF … Toxoplasma gondii PCR … were negative.”  
4. Considered viral encephalopathy (EBV, HSV) but excluded after negative PCRs — “CSF … EBV PCR, herpes simplex virus (HSV) 1 and 2 PCR, and … VDRL tests were negative.”  
5. Considered stroke given focal white matter lesions but deemed unlikely due to subacute progression and imaging pattern — “Our initial differential diagnosis included … stroke.”  
6. Diagnosed PML based on the combination of progressive neurologic decline, multifocal demyelinating-appearing white matter lesions on MRI, and rising CSF JC viral load — “the constellation of findings including rising CSF JC viral loads, radiographic imaging, and neurologic changes made PML secondary to JC virus the most unifying diagnosis.”
